passage:
Tuesday: Ojas got stuck on the fraction word problem and threw his pencil down. Harish sir came over. "What have you tried?" "Nothing works." "Try drawing it," Harish sir said, and moved on.
Wednesday: Ojas tried drawing pizzas. Wrong. Then counting in steps. Wrong. Then a number line, and it worked. Harish sir crouched by his desk. "You tried three different ways, and when the first two didn't work, you switched. That's exactly how people get good at maths."
Friday: When Harish sir offered a harder bonus sheet, Ojas's hand shot up first. "Can I try the number line on these?" He got four out of six, and he was grinning.

qa.q: What method finally worked for Ojas on Wednesday?
qa.a: A number line.

qa.q: Why was Ojas's hand the first to shoot up on Friday?
qa.a: Harish sir's praise showed him that switching methods is how people get good, so he felt confident and eager, seeing a harder sheet as a chance rather than a risk.

qa.q: What made Harish sir's praise work well?
qa.a: It named exactly what Ojas did, trying three ways and switching, rather than calling him clever, so he knew what to repeat.

qa.q: What would change if Harish sir had only said "Good boy, you're clever"?
qa.a: Ojas might not know what helped, and could even avoid the bonus sheet in case it made him look less clever.

grounding: A teacher praises a child's strategy switching, and the child begins seeking harder problems.

passage: Imran, you asked how to encourage the weaker ones in your class. Let me tell you about a girl called Pinki, from my first year teaching in Nagpur, when the children called me Usha teacher. She was nine and she hated long division. One day I watched her try it the book way and fail, then try splitting the number into hundreds and tens and fail, then try guessing and checking, and get it right. Before, I'd have said "good girl, clever girl". That day I said, "Pinki, you tried three ways and didn't give up. That's how you got it." She looked at me as if no one had ever said that to her. The next week she asked for the hard sums. Praise what they did, beta, not what they are.

qa.q: What three ways did Pinki try for long division?
qa.a: The book way, splitting the number into hundreds and tens, and guessing and checking.

qa.q: Why did Pinki look at Usha teacher as if no one had ever said that?
qa.a: She was surprised and moved to be praised for her persistence rather than her cleverness; it showed her that her effort mattered.

qa.q: What choice does Usha urge Imran to make in class?
qa.a: To praise what the children do, their methods and persistence, rather than what they are, so they reach for harder work.

qa.q: How might Imran use this story with the weaker students?
qa.a: Imran might watch for a child trying different approaches and name it aloud, helping that child see progress as something they can build.

grounding: An elder teacher recalls praising a child's methods and persistence, after which the child sought harder problems.

passage: The Class 6 room at the government school had fifty-two students and one fan, and Francis sir had only ten minutes before the bell. Samir was still bent over the geometry problem most had skipped, having tried measuring with a broken ruler, then folding the paper, then drawing a grid on the back. Francis sir, squeezing between benches with forty notebooks still to check, stopped anyway. "Samir, show me." Samir showed the grid. "You tried folding, and when that didn't work you made a grid. That was smart work, not luck." The bell rang. Samir packed slowly, still looking at the grid. The next day, Samir came to the staffroom door with another problem from the back of the book. "Sir, I want to try this one."

qa.q: What did Samir draw on the back of the paper?
qa.a: A grid.

qa.q: Why did Samir pack slowly, still looking at the grid?
qa.a: Samir seemed proud and thoughtful, taking in that the grid was good work, not luck, and that switching methods had paid off.

qa.q: Which choice by Francis sir mattered most under the time pressure?
qa.a: Stopping for a moment despite the crowded room and the notebooks, and naming Samir's exact strategy rather than just saying "well done".

qa.q: What would change if Francis sir had walked past without stopping?
qa.a: Samir might have left without knowing the grid idea was valuable, and might not have come to the staffroom asking for a harder problem.

grounding: Despite a crowded class and little time, a teacher praises a child's switch of strategy, and the child seeks more challenge.

passage: In the Class 3 room of a Hyderabad school, Aparna had been stuck on the same puzzle for ten minutes: move matchsticks to make three triangles out of nine sticks. First she laid them in a row. Then she tried a star. Then she drew it on paper, rubbed it out, and tried again, tongue between her teeth. Finally the three triangles clicked. Rukmini Ma'am came over. "Aparna, I watched you. You tried a row, then a star, then you drew it out. When one way didn't work, you changed the way. That's why you got it." Aparna looked at her matchsticks, then up. "Can I try the harder one? The four triangles?" Rukmini Ma'am smiled and handed her the card.

qa.q: How many matchsticks did Aparna have to work with?
qa.a: Nine sticks.

qa.q: Why does Aparna ask for the harder puzzle right away?
qa.a: Hearing that changing her approach is what worked made her feel she could do it again, so a harder puzzle seemed exciting rather than risky.

qa.q: Which part of Rukmini Ma'am's praise mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Naming the exact steps, row, star, drawing, and the switch between them; it tells Aparna that her methods and persistence, not luck, solved the puzzle.

qa.q: How might a classmate who gave up early feel hearing Rukmini Ma'am's words?
qa.a: That classmate might realise that getting stuck is normal and that trying different ways is what worked, and feel encouraged to try again.

grounding: A teacher praises a child for changing methods until one worked, and the child immediately seeks a harder challenge.

passage:
"Mausi, I got it! The kite-string sum!"
Ishita Mausi put down her tea. "The one you called impossible at lunch?"
"Yes! First I tried adding, wrong. Then I drew the kite and the string, still wrong. Then I made a table like you do on your board."
"Show me." Mausi read the page slowly. "Aditi, look at what you did. You didn't stop when adding failed. You drew it. When the drawing didn't work, you changed again. The table worked because you'd already ruled out two ways."
"So I'm good at maths?"
"You're getting better at maths, because you kept changing your way in. That's how it grows. I see it in my Class 5 kids too."
Aditi flipped to a fresh page. "Then give me the tough one from your box."

qa.a: Adding, drawing the kite and the string, and making a table.

qa.a: Aditi feels proud and excited, and is checking whether success means a fixed talent; it hints at a pull toward labels, which Mausi gently turns toward effort.

qa.q: What choice does Ishita Mausi make in her answer, and why does it help?
qa.a: She describes each method and says ability grows by changing approaches; that makes Aditi want the tough problem instead of protecting a label.

qa.q: How might Ishita Mausi feel when Aditi asks for the tough one?
qa.a: Ishita Mausi is probably delighted 😊, seeing that praise for the process has made a challenge feel inviting rather than scary.

grounding: An aunt who is a teacher praises a child's switching of methods, teaching that ability grows, and the child asks for a harder problem.

passage: In Class 6 there was a word problem about trains that I could not do. I tried adding. Wrong. I tried drawing the trains on paper. Still wrong. Then I made a table with the times. passage:
Class 5 note, Wednesday

Sachin has been stuck on long division for weeks. Today I watched him try one sum three ways: first repeated subtraction, then drawing groups, then the standard method with a small grid. The third way worked. Instead of saying "good boy" or "you're clever," I told him exactly what I saw: "You kept trying new methods when the first ones didn't work, and that's why you got it."

He looked surprised, then pleased. In the afternoon, when I offered an easy sheet or a harder one, he picked the harder one for the first time. He got two wrong and just said, "I'll try the grid."

I will keep noting what he does, not what he is.

— Reena

qa.q: How many methods did Sachin try on the sum?
qa.a: Three: repeated subtraction, drawing groups, and the standard method with a small grid.

qa.q: What did Sachin's choice of the harder sheet suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt more confident and less afraid of mistakes after being praised for trying different methods.

qa.q: Why is Reena's praise more helpful than 'you're clever'?
qa.a: It names the specific effort and strategies Sachin used, showing him that trying new ways leads to success.

qa.q: How might Sachin see his own mistakes now?
qa.a: He seems to see them as a reason to try another method, like the grid, rather than as a sign that he's not clever.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, how specific praise for a child's changing methods helps him believe ability grows and seek harder work.

passage:
Dear Diary,

Today in art, I was painting a tree and the leaves looked like green blobs. I tried a thin brush. Worse. I tried dabbing with a sponge. Better. Then I tried a toothbrush flick, like Seema ma'am showed last month. Leaves!

Seema ma'am came round and said, "Darshan, you didn't give up. You tried three tools and found what works. That's how painters get better." I felt happy all afternoon 😊

She didn't say I'm good at painting. She said I tried. And I think that's better, because I can always try, even if I'm not good yet.

Tomorrow I'm going to try a sky with the sponge. Skies are hard. But that's okay.

Darshan

qa.q: Which tool gave Darshan leaves that looked right?
qa.a: The toothbrush flick.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after Seema ma'am's words?
qa.a: Darshan felt happy all afternoon and more confident to try harder things, like skies.

qa.q: What made Seema ma'am's praise useful for Darshan?
qa.a: It pointed out the effort and the tools tried, so Darshan learned that trying can always help, even without being good yet.

qa.q: How might Seema ma'am feel reading that Darshan wants to try a hard sky?
qa.a: Seema ma'am would likely feel proud that her specific praise helped Darshan seek a new challenge.

grounding: It shows a teacher praising a child's changing strategies, which teaches that ability grows with effort and encourages challenge seeking.

passage:
In the Nandgaon village school, Farhan, ten, was stuck sharing 36 mangoes among 4 families. He drew mangoes. Too many. He counted in fours on his fingers and lost count. Then he remembered the multiplication table on the wall and worked backwards: 4 times 9 is 36.
Bhavna Ma'am came by and looked at his slate, covered in crossed-out mangoes and finger marks.
She didn't say “clever boy.” She said, “You tried three different ways. When drawing didn't work, you changed your plan. That's how you got it.”
Farhan looked at his slate as if seeing it for the first time.
The next day there was a hard sum on the board, and he put his hand up first. “Ma'am, can I try it? I'll try a different way if it doesn't work.”

qa.q: How many mangoes were being shared?
qa.a: 36 mangoes were being shared among 4 families.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when Bhavna Ma'am described what he did?
qa.a: He felt surprised and proud, seeing his messy slate as proof that his changing strategies worked.

qa.q: Why was Bhavna Ma'am's praise effective?
qa.a: She praised his specific strategies and persistence instead of cleverness, which taught him that ability grows with effort.

qa.q: How might Bhavna Ma'am feel seeing Farhan volunteer for the hard sum?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and encouraged that her praise made him seek a challenge.

grounding: The passage shows a teacher praising a child's changing strategies rather than cleverness, and the child starting to seek challenges.

passage:
In a school in Mexico City, Omar, nine, was building a bridge from paper and tape that had to hold ten coins. His first bridge collapsed at three coins. His second held five.
He was about to give up when he noticed his friend's bridge had folded paper, like a fan. He tried folding his. It held eight coins. Then he added a second layer. It held twelve.
His teacher, Ms Camila, crouched down. “Omar, I watched you. When the flat bridge fell, you didn't quit. You looked at a different design, tried folding, then added a layer. That's why it worked.”
Omar grinned. “So I'm good at bridges?”
“You're good at trying new ways,” she said. “That's better.”
On Friday, when they had to build a tower, Omar picked the hardest design on the sheet.

qa.q: How many coins did Omar's final bridge hold?
qa.a: It held twelve coins.

qa.q: How did Omar feel when Ms Camila explained what he did?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, grinning at the specific praise of his methods.

qa.q: Why did Ms Camila's praise support challenge seeking?
qa.a: She named his strategies and persistence rather than a talent, so Omar learned that effort and new methods pay off.

qa.q: How might Ms Camila feel when Omar picks the hardest design on Friday?
qa.a: She would probably feel delighted that her process praise made him more willing to take on challenges.

grounding: The passage shows a teacher praising a child's changing methods rather than talent, and the child choosing harder challenges afterwards.

passage:
At the Saturday chess club in the community hall, Alka, eleven, had lost three games in a row to Ria. In the fourth game she sat very still, thinking longer before each move. She tried castling early. She protected her queen. She lost again, but only after forty moves.
Coach Naveen came over as she packed her pieces. “Alka, can I tell you what I saw? In game one you moved fast. In game four you slowed down, you planned your castling and you guarded your queen. That's why it lasted forty moves.”
Alka frowned. “But I still lost.”
“You did. But you changed your strategy, and it worked better. That's how players get stronger.”
Alka looked at the board. Then she walked over to Ria. “Can we play again next Saturday? I want to try something else.”

qa.q: How many moves did Alka's fourth game last?
qa.a: It lasted forty moves.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when she said “But I still lost”?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and a bit discouraged, focused on the loss rather than her progress.

qa.q: Why was Coach Naveen's feedback effective?
qa.a: He named specific changes in her strategy and linked them to the better result, showing that skill grows with effort.

qa.q: How might Ria see Alka asking for a rematch?
qa.a: Ria might feel respected and a little surprised that Alka wants to play again after four losses.

grounding: The passage shows a coach praising a child's strategy changes rather than talent, and the child seeking another challenge.

passage:
I'm Sangeeta, and I volunteer on Thursdays in the Class 4 room at my son's school. Last week I saw something I keep thinking about.

Then, when she held up the challenge card, the hard one, his hand went up first. I can't say for sure what was in his head. But he looked like someone who wanted another go.

"Noor, you're stuck on your crossword and want to give up? Let me tell you about a boy in my class, back when I, your Salma Nani, was a teacher.
It was the monsoon, and the classroom roof dripped into a bucket. Irfan was nine and hated long division. One day he tried it the book's way. Wrong. He tried estimating first. Wrong. Then he broke the big number into smaller chunks, and it came out right.
I didn't tell him he was clever. I said, 'Irfan, you tried three ways, and you didn't stop. That chunking idea was yours, and it worked.'
He looked at me as if no one had ever noticed how he thought.
The next week, when I offered the extra-hard sums as a choice, he took them first. He got some wrong. He didn't care. He wanted to see which way would work."

qa.a: He seemed surprised and deeply pleased, as if no one had ever noticed how he thought.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows that Salma's praise worked?
qa.a: The next week Irfan chose the extra-hard sums first and didn't mind getting some wrong, because he wanted to test which method would work.

qa.q: How might Irfan's classmates have seen him after that?
qa.a: They might have noticed him taking on the hardest sums without fear and seen that trying different methods pays off.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a teacher praising a child's different methods and persistence, after which he chose harder sums.

passage:
The power went out halfway through the monsoon fractions class, and rain drummed so loudly on the tin roof that Manjula Ma'am had to walk desk to desk instead of teaching from the board.
Tarun was stuck on the pizza problem. First he drew circles, but they came out uneven. Then he tried folding a strip of paper. That didn't work either. Finally he lined up twelve chalk marks and circled groups of three and four.
Manjula Ma'am crouched by his desk with her phone torch. "You tried circles, then paper, then lines. When one way failed, you switched. That's why you got it."
Tarun looked at his messy page. "So being stuck is part of it?"
"It is. Want to try the tougher one on page forty?"
He nodded and turned the page before the lights came back.

qa.a: She named each method Tarun tried and linked switching to success, which made him willing to take on the tougher problem.

grounding: A teacher praises a child's switching of methods during a power cut, and the child chooses a harder problem next.
